impacts.caseName: Dental Monitoring SAS v. Align Technology, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board's precedential Penumbra framework—holding that Dynamic Drinkware's written description analysis for provisional application priority dates applies only under pre-AIA law and not under AIA § 102(d)(2)—is correct.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the PTAB's obviousness determination, questioning the Board's Penumbra rule that a reference patent automatically receives its provisional application's filing date for AIA prior art purposes without a Dynamic Drinkware-style written description analysis. This decision could restrict when published patents qualify as prior art based on provisional filing dates under the AIA.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit because references used against their patents in IPR proceedings may lose earlier effective dates if their provisional applications do not adequately describe the relied-upon subject matter, potentially reducing the prior art available to challengers.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies challenging patents in IPR proceedings face additional hurdles in establishing prior art dates, potentially making it harder and more expensive to invalidate patents held by competitors or NPEs.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement for method claims requires the specification to enable the full scope of the claimed genus of compounds, or whether a narrower standard applies when the method claim includes a treatment limitation.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied Eli Lilly's petition for rehearing en banc, letting stand a panel decision upholding Teva's broad method claims for treating headache with anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies. Judge Dyk dissented, arguing the panel's holding undermines enablement standards for method claims and is contrary to Supreme Court precedent, allowing overly broad claims to stand.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical and biotech patent holders benefit from a more permissive enablement standard for method-of-treatment claims, allowing broader genus claims that cover entire classes of therapeutic compounds to survive validity challenges.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar manufacturers face broader patent barriers to market entry, as competitors can obtain and enforce sweeping method claims that may cover compounds the patentee never actually developed, potentially delaying competition.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' in the patents to the licensee such that the licensee could sue for infringement without joining the patent owner, and whether the agreement automatically terminated when the licensee shifted its business to patent enforcement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that TexasLDPC's exclusive license from Texas A&M University conveyed all substantial rights and did not terminate when the company shifted to enforcement activities. The court found that the licensee had standing to sue for infringement in its own name without joining the university.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees and patent assertion entities benefit from clarity that shifting business operations to patent enforcement does not automatically terminate license agreements, and that comprehensive exclusive licenses confer standing to sue independently.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a potentially powerful defense—challenging standing by arguing the patent owner must be joined—when the exclusive license agreement is sufficiently broad, making it harder to dismiss infringement suits on procedural grounds.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding Versata's trade secret damages expert testimony and in overturning the jury's breach of contract damages award related to Ford's development of competing software using Versata's licensed trade secrets.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously excluded damages models. The court also reversed the district court's post-trial reduction of the breach of contract jury award, reinstating the original verdict. The court affirmed Ford's liability for trade secret misappropriation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software developers and trade secret holders benefit from broader acceptance of damages models in misappropriation cases and from the reinstatement of jury damage awards, strengthening enforcement of trade secret and licensing agreements.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop in-house replacements for licensed software face heightened misappropriation liability and potentially larger damages awards, increasing the risk and cost of transitioning away from third-party technology.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to non-uniform signal constellations used in digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents directed to non-uniform constellations, finding unresolved factual disputes at Alice step two, while affirming eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents. The court affirmed the jury's infringement and damages findings for the eligible claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies accused of infringement benefit from the court's willingness to scrutinize eligibility even after summary judgment, providing another opportunity to challenge abstract-idea-based patents in communications technology.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in digital communications and standards-essential technology face uncertainty as eligibility determinations may be vacated and remanded for further factual inquiry, delaying resolution of infringement disputes and potentially reducing patent value.

impacts.caseName: Range of Motion Products, LLC v. Armaid Company Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Egyptian Goddess improperly shifted the design patent infringement analysis to focus on differences rather than overall similarity, and whether claim construction of design patents involving functionality presents factual questions for the jury.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied rehearing en banc, maintaining its Egyptian Goddess framework for design patent infringement. The concurrence defended the ordinary observer test as properly accounting for both similarities and differences, while the dissent (Chief Judge Moore and three others) argued the framework improperly focuses on dissimilarity and resolves factual functionality questions at summary judgment rather than trial.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the continued framework that permits summary judgment of non-infringement in design patent cases when differences between designs are sufficiently clear, reducing litigation costs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Design patent holders face a continued risk that courts will grant summary judgment against them by focusing on differences rather than overall similarity, and that functionality determinations will be resolved without jury involvement, potentially undervaluing design patents.

impacts.caseName: Board of Regents of the University of Texas v. Boston Scientific Corp.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the asserted claims of a patent directed to drug-releasing biodegradable fiber implants were anticipated by prior art and whether the accused drug-eluting stent systems infringed the asserted claims.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury verdict in favor of UT, holding that Boston Scientific was entitled to judgment as a matter of law on both invalidity (anticipation) and non-infringement of claims covering drug-releasing biodegradable fiber implants used in coronary stents. The court found the prior art anticipated the claims and that BSC's products did not infringe.
impacts.positiveImplications: Medical device manufacturers benefit from the reversal of a potentially large damages verdict, reinforcing that prior art defenses and non-infringement arguments can prevail even after adverse jury verdicts in patent cases involving life sciences technology.
impacts.negativeImplications: Universities and research institutions asserting patents against major device manufacturers face heightened risk that appellate courts will overturn favorable jury verdicts, potentially diminishing the value of their patent portfolios and licensing revenue.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has subject-matter jurisdiction over a dispute concerning interpretation of a patent settlement agreement's contingent payment provision, or whether it is a state-law contract question for the regional circuit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit transferred the case to the Fifth Circuit, holding it lacked jurisdiction because the dispute over whether asserted claims 'survived' an ex parte reexamination was fundamentally a state-law contract interpretation issue, not a patent law question. This clarifies jurisdictional boundaries for patent settlement disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies structuring patent settlements benefit from clarity that post-settlement contract disputes will be heard in regional circuits applying state contract law, potentially providing more predictable and favorable forums for contract interpretation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent litigants who assumed the Federal Circuit would interpret settlement terms tied to patent proceedings may face unexpected jurisdictional transfers, adding delay and uncertainty to resolution of settlement disputes.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims reciting a communications apparatus with a coupler matching transmitter impedance to the 'characteristic impedance of the air' are indefinite, and whether the claims satisfy the enablement requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's indefiniteness ruling but affirmed the final judgment of invalidity on alternative enablement grounds, holding that the patent's claims covering wireless transmission technology were not enabled because the specification failed to teach how to practice the invention across the full scope of the claims. This provides guidance on the interplay between indefiniteness and enablement defenses.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the court's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative grounds even when the primary invalidity theory fails, providing multiple avenues to challenge overly broad wireless technology patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in wireless and communications technology face the risk that claims surviving indefiniteness challenges may still be invalidated for lack of enablement, requiring more detailed specifications to support broad claims.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court provided sufficient reasoning in denying a defendant's motions for Rule 11 sanctions and attorneys' fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 after the asserted patent claims were found invalid under § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's denial of sanctions and attorneys' fees, holding that the court's order lacked sufficient detail for meaningful appellate review. The case involved a patent holder that continued to assert claims despite multiple PTO § 101 rejections of related applications and a prior court invalidation of a related patent, raising significant questions about exceptional-case findings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants who prevail on § 101 invalidity grounds benefit from enhanced ability to recover fees when patent holders assert claims despite substantial prior art and eligibility rejections, deterring frivolous patent assertions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders and their counsel face increased risk of fee-shifting and sanctions when asserting patents with related applications that were rejected on eligibility grounds, requiring more careful pre-suit analysis of § 101 risks.

impacts.caseName: VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in dismissing a patent infringement complaint without leave to amend, awarding § 285 attorneys' fees, and sanctioning plaintiff's counsel under 28 U.S.C. § 1927.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the dismissal with prejudice and the § 285 fee award against VDPP, holding the proposed amended complaint was futile and the case was exceptional. The court also affirmed sanctions against plaintiff's counsel for unreasonably and vexatiously multiplying proceedings. This reinforces accountability for filing meritless patent infringement suits.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from strong precedent supporting fee-shifting and attorney sanctions in cases where patent holders file meritless infringement suits, particularly when complaints fail to adequately allege pre-suit notice for damages.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent assertion entities and their counsel face significant financial exposure from sanctions and fee awards when filing infringement complaints that fail basic pleading standards, increasing the cost of bringing marginal patent claims.

impacts.caseName: Archroma U.S., Inc. v. Department of Commerce
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce's regulatory 15-day deadline for domestic interested parties to indicate intent to participate in antidumping duty sunset reviews conflicts with the governing statute, which is silent on such a deadline.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade, holding that Commerce's regulation requiring domestic interested parties to file within 15 days of initiation of a sunset review was a permissible exercise of agency authority, as the statute was silent on the filing deadline. This preserves Commerce's procedural framework for antidumping duty sunset reviews.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic manufacturers and producers seeking continuation of antidumping duties benefit from a clear, predictable regulatory timeline, and the decision upholds Commerce's authority to administer trade remedy proceedings efficiently.
impacts.negativeImplications: Importers and foreign exporters face the continued enforcement of a strict 15-day participation deadline that, if missed by domestic parties, could lead to automatic revocation of antidumping duties, but the ruling makes such missed deadlines less likely by validating the regulatory framework.

impacts.caseName: Exelixis, Inc. v. MSN Laboratories Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the asserted claims of patents covering crystalline and amorphous forms of cabozantinib (L)-malate satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a) when the specification primarily describes crystalline forms.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding of adequate written description for patents covering cabozantinib malate salt formulations used in cancer treatment (Cabometyx®), rejecting the generic manufacturer's argument that the specification failed to support claims encompassing amorphous forms. This decision protects Exelixis's patent portfolio through 2030.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies benefit from the court's validation of patent claims covering both crystalline and amorphous salt forms, strengthening patent protection for blockbuster drugs and delaying generic competition.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic pharmaceutical manufacturers face continued patent barriers to market entry for cabozantinib products, as the broad written description standard makes it harder to invalidate formulation patents covering multiple solid-state forms.

impacts.caseName: NCS Multistage Inc. v. Nine Energy Service, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the claim term 'internal diameter' in patents related to oil and gas wellbore float tools, and whether claim construction errors affected the infringement and validity findings.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the infringement and validity judgment in a dispute between oilfield service competitors over float tool patents used in horizontal well casing operations. The case turned on claim construction of 'internal diameter,' a critical term defining the structural relationship between tool components.
impacts.positiveImplications: Oilfield service companies benefit from the court's careful scrutiny of claim construction in mechanical patents, ensuring that overly broad constructions do not sweep in non-infringing competitor products.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the oil and gas industry face the risk that infringement verdicts may be vacated when claim terms are not precisely construed, requiring remand and potentially years of additional litigation.
